c: Cycle Cart, a proposed mobile coffee cart that would serve commuters at a busy train station
s: You and your partners want to open Cycle Cart, a bike-powered coffee cart at a train station where about 4,000 commuters pass each weekday morning. You have $14,000 in savings and are considering whether to start with a cart, a leased kiosk inside the station, or a food truck.

The small business advisor (judge) is a volunteer from a local business development center. The advisor wants to hear what business idea you have, who the customers are, what it will cost to start, and which of the three formats you would choose and why.
You have 7 minutes to present your concept, compare the alternatives with pros and cons, and describe your first steps.
f: Savings available: $14,000; a loan of up to $10,000 is possible
Cart: about $9,000 to build plus a $600 annual vendor permit
Kiosk: $3,200 a month rent and $18,000 in build-out costs
Food truck: $48,000 used plus $2,400 a month for parking and permits
Estimated sales: 120 cups a day at $4.25 with a cost of $1.35 per cup
m: a conference room at the business center
n: Describes the customer, the need and what makes the idea different
Compares the cart, kiosk and truck on cost, risk, and revenue potential
Calculates a simple daily profit (about $348 before rent and labor) and break-even idea
Explains how the cart fits the savings and loan limits
Names the permits and licenses that must be handled before opening
Lays out the first 30 days of steps
q: What happens if rainy days cut sales in half?
How did you decide that people will pay $4.25?
Which of these three formats could you walk away from if it fails?

c: TutorLoop, a startup app that matches high school students with college tutors
s: You founded TutorLoop eight months ago. The app has 1,900 student users and 240 tutors, and it earns a 15 percent fee on each paid session. You are seeking $75,000 from a local angel investor to hire a developer and run a marketing campaign. The investor has offered it in exchange for 20 percent of the company, but you were hoping to keep more ownership.

The investor (judge) wants to know whether the business is real, how it will use the money, and what other ways you have thought about raising funds. The investor will interrupt with questions as you present.
You have 7 minutes to present your case, compare financing alternatives and recommend what you will do.
f: Users: 1,900 students, 240 tutors, 410 paid sessions per month
Average session price: $24; the company keeps 15% of each
Monthly costs: about $2,900 for hosting, payment fees and part-time support
Investor offer: $75,000 for 20% ownership
Alternatives: a $25,000 bank loan at 8.5%, a crowdfunding campaign, or growing from revenue
d: present your pitch and funding plan
n: Explains the business model and its monthly numbers (about $1,476 in fees against $2,900 in costs)
Describes the risks and rewards of entrepreneurship honestly
Compares equity, a loan, crowdfunding and slow growth with pros and cons
Explains what the $75,000 will buy and the results it should produce
Mentions legal matters, such as protecting minors' data and a tutor contractor agreement
Recommends a decision and the terms to negotiate
q: Why should I believe students will keep using it?
What does 20 percent really cost you in the long run?
How will you protect the privacy of high school students?

c: GreenGrip, a startup that wants to sell recycled-rubber phone cases
s: GreenGrip has a prototype phone case made from recycled bike tires. Friends love it, but you have no sales data. You can spend about $1,500 on research before deciding whether to order 1,000 cases for $9,000. Your teacher wants to see how you would test the idea before spending on a large order.

The teacher (judge) will play a skeptical mentor and wants you to explain how you would discover whether people will buy the case, what research methods you would use, how you would use what you learn, and how you would decide whether to move forward.
You have 7 minutes to present your research plan, compare the alternatives with pros and cons, and recommend next steps.
f: Research budget: $1,500; production order: 1,000 cases for $9,000 ($9 each)
Planned retail price: $24; competing cases range from $12 to $40
A survey of 40 friends: 31 said they would buy one
A pre-order page would cost about $200 to build; a booth at a weekend market would cost $120
Target customer: students and commuters aged 15 to 30
d: present your research and decision plan
n: Explains why a friends-only survey is biased and what better evidence looks like
Compares research methods: pre-orders, market booth, online survey and competitor study
Describes who the customer is and what problem the case solves
Sets a clear decision rule, such as 50 pre-orders before ordering
Estimates the margin ($15 per case at $24) and the break-even number (600 cases)
Names a smaller first order or a supplier alternative as a fallback
q: What result would make you cancel the whole idea?
How could the survey of your friends mislead you?
What would you do if pre-orders came in at half your goal?

c: Spark Photo Booth, a new business renting photo booths for weddings and school dances
s: Spark Photo Booth has been open for six months and is booked nearly every weekend in spring. The co-owners want to buy two more booths for $11,000 each and hire a part-time attendant. They are asking a local bank for a $22,000 loan. The loan officer has questions about the business plan, the legal setup and the risks.

The loan officer (judge) wants to understand how you run the business day to day, how you will manage employees and records, what insurance and legal protections you have, and what happens if bookings fall during the off-season.
You have 7 minutes to present the business, compare the choices (buy two booths, buy one, or lease), and recommend one.
f: Current booth rental: $450 per event, 31 events in six months
Operating costs: supplies and travel about $60 per event; insurance $55 a month
Two new booths: $22,000 total; one new booth: $11,000; leasing: $380 a month per booth
Off-season (July to September) typically has only 2 or 3 events a month
The business is an LLC with two co-owners and no employees yet
n: Explains the day-to-day activities of running the venture, including scheduling and customer service
Describes the business structure (LLC) and why liability protection matters
Compares buying two, buying one and leasing, with pros and cons including seasonality
Shows that revenue ($13,950 so far) can cover loan payments with a safety margin
Discusses insurance, contracts and employee requirements for the part-time attendant
Recommends the most prudent option and a plan for the slow season
q: How would you pay the loan during the three slow months?
What happens if a booth is damaged at a client's event?
Why do you need two booths rather than one?

c: Harvest Box, a startup that sells weekly boxes of locally grown produce
s: Harvest Box buys vegetables from six local farms and delivers weekly boxes to 140 subscribers. The founders are about to sign a contract with a large office complex to deliver 200 boxes a week. A friend mentioned that they may need a business license, a food handling permit, a contract review and the right kind of insurance, and that the business is currently operating as a sole proprietorship.
The attorney (judge) has agreed to give you a short consultation. The attorney wants to know what you are doing now, what you plan to do, and how you would manage legal risk as the business grows.
You have 7 minutes to explain your situation, compare the legal options available to you, and recommend what to do before signing the new contract.
f: Current structure: sole proprietorship owned by one founder; the co-founder is paid as a contractor
Revenue: $9,800 a month from 140 subscribers
The office contract is for 12 months and would add about $5,400 a month
Insurance: none beyond a general home policy
Legal costs: forming an LLC is about $500; a contract review is $350; business insurance is about $900 a year
n: Identifies the risks of a sole proprietorship, including unlimited personal liability
Compares staying as is, forming an LLC and forming a corporation with pros and cons
Lists licenses, permits and food-safety requirements to check
Explains why a contract review and liability insurance matter before signing
Distinguishes an employee from an independent contractor
Recommends the order of steps and the costs, about $1,750 in total
q: What would happen to your personal savings if a customer got sick?
Should the co-founder be an owner, an employee or a contractor?
What clause in the office contract worries you the most?
